title: ON Semiconductor to buy Ferric for $600M to strengthen AI power delivery
subtitle: The cash deal — with up to $175M in revenue-linked earnouts — folds Ferric's integrated voltage regulator technology into onsemi's AI data-center stack, as power delivery joins interconnect and memory on the list of chip-industry rollup targets.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: ON Semiconductor (onsemi) agreed to acquire Ferric for $600 million in cash, plus up to $175 million in additional payments tied to revenue milestones. Ferric makes integrated voltage regulator technology that sits physically close to AI accelerators and delivers power at the voltages and transient response that modern GPUs and custom AI silicon demand. The deal, announced during the week, folds Ferric's product lines and engineering team into onsemi's expanding AI data-center portfolio. Markets reacted positively — onsemi shares traded higher on the day of the announcement, with analysts citing the deal as a credible bolt-on in a segment where onsemi has publicly identified AI power as a growth priority.

Power delivery is the quietly critical half of the AI compute stack. A modern GPU can draw a kilowatt-plus at voltages under one volt, with current transients of hundreds of amps on sub-microsecond timescales. Classical discrete-component power delivery cannot keep up without either throttling the chip or wasting a significant fraction of input power as heat. Integrated voltage regulators that live in the same package as the accelerator or directly adjacent to it are the industry's answer, and Ferric is one of the specialist suppliers in that space. Owning that capability inside a broader power-semi vendor is the kind of integration that becomes valuable when hyperscalers want single-vendor sourcing for their next-generation reference designs.

The deal fits the week's broader pattern of AI-infrastructure consolidation. Marvell's proposed $115B acquisition of Lumentum targets optical interconnect; Analog Devices has just closed its Alif Semiconductor deal; and multiple reported rounds and rumors cluster around power, packaging, and advanced cooling. These are the parts of the AI compute system that don't get press releases from model labs, but they are where incumbents and specialists are being bought and welded together because the GPUs they feed will be shipped at scales that reward vertical control.

A takeaway for learners: when a company's growth story depends on 'AI,' look at whether the actual products touch the AI compute stack at a layer where real engineering problems are being solved. Ferric is a small company with a specific technical edge in a hard physics problem — delivering clean power at modern AI silicon's voltage and current profile. That is a qualitatively different story from a company that wraps an API and calls it AI. If you want to understand AI as an industry, learn to tell the difference between the layers where engineering is being done and the layers where branding is being applied.
